#Text=It has an operation pretty strange, which is, that when it is
#Text= new it will make them that eat it like drunk, sick and spue; and this
#Text= only when it is sown in some Grounds, for in all it will not have this
#Text= effect: and being old, none will have it.
#Text=Minere, a small seed.
#Text=Boumas,
#Text= we call them Garavances.
#Text=Tolla, a seed used to make Oyl, with which
#Text= they anoint themselves; and sometimes they will parch it and eat it
#Text= with Jaggory, a kind of brown Sugar.
#Text=And thus much of their Corn.
#Text=CHAP.
#Text=IV.
#Text=Of their Fruits, and Trees
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= [Great variety of Fruits, and delicious.]
#Text=Of Fruits here are great
#Text= plenty and variety, and far more might be if they did esteem or
#Text=nourish them.
#Text=Pleasant Fruits to eat ripe they care not at all to do,
#Text= They look only after those that may fill the Belly, and satisfie their
#Text= hunger when their Corn is spent, or to make it go the further.
#Text=These
#Text= onely they plant, the other Fruits of Pleasure plant themselves, the
#Text= seeds of the ripe Fruits shedding and falling on the ground naturally
#Text= spring up again.
#Text=They have all Fruits that grow in India.
#Text=Most sorts
#Text= of these delicious Fruits they gather before they be ripe, and boyl
#Text= them to make Carrees, to use the Portuguez word, that is somewhat to
#Text= eat with and relish their Rice.
#Text=[The best Fruits, where-ever they
#Text= grow, reserved for the King.]
#Text=But wheresoever there is any Fruit
#Text= better than ordinary, the Ponudecarso, or Officers of the Countrey,
#Text= will tie a string about the Tree in the Kings Name with three knots
#Text= on the end thereof, and then, no man, not the Owner himself, dares
#Text= presume under pain of some great punishment, if not death, to touch
#Text= them.
#Text=And when they are ripe, they are wrapped in white cloth, and
#Text= carried to him who is Governour of that Countrey wherein they grow:
#Text= and if they be without any defect or blemish, then being wrapped up
#Text= again in white cloth, he presents them to the King.
#Text=But the owner in
#Text= whose Ground they grow is paid nothing at all for them: it is well
#Text= if he be not compelled to carry them himself into the bargain unto
#Text=like an Hedg-hog, and of a greenish colour; there are in them Seeds
#Text= or Kernels, or Eggs as the Chingulayes call them, which lie dispersed
#Text= in the Fruit like Seeds in a Cucumber.
#Text=They usually gather them before
#Text= they be full ripe, boreing an hole in them, and feeling of the Kernel,
#Text= they know if they be ripe enough for their purpose.
#Text=Then being cut in
#Text= pieces they boil them, and eat to save Rice and fill their Bellies;
#Text= they eat them as we would do Turnips or Cabbage, and tast and smell
#Text= much like the latter: one may suffice six or seven men.
#Text=When they
#Text= are ripe they are sweet and good to eat raw.
#Text=The Kernels do very
#Text= much resemble Chesnuts both in colour and tast, and are almost as
#Text= good: the poor people will boyl them or roast them in the embers,
#Text= there being usually a good heap of them lying in a corner by the
#Text= fire side; and when they go a Journey, they will put them in a bag
#Text= for their Provisions by the way.
#Text=One Jack may contain three pints
#Text= or two quarts of these seeds or kernels.
#Text=When they cut these Jacks,
#Text= there comes running out a white thick substance like tar, and will
#Text= stick just like Birdlime, which the Boyes make use of to catch Birds,
#Text= which they call Cola, or bloud of the Cos.
#Text=Some will mix this with
#Text= the flower of Rice, and it will eat like Eggs.
#Text=[Jombo.]
#Text=Another Fruit there is which I never saw in any other Parts
#Text= of India, they call it Jombo.
#Text=In tast it is like to an Apple, full
#Text= of Juice, and pleasant to the Palate, and not unwholsom to the Body,
#Text= and to the Eye no Fruit more amiable, being white, and delicately
#Text= coloured with red, as if it were painted.
#Text=[Other fruits found in the Woods.]
#Text=Also in the wild Woods are
#Text= several sorts of pretty Fruits, as Murros, round in shape, and as
#Text= big as a Cherry, and sweet to the tast; Dongs, nearest like to a
#Text= black Cherry.
#Text=Ambelo  '  s like to Barberries.
#Text=Carolla cabella, Cabela
#Text= pooke, and Polla  '  s, these are like to little Plums, and very well
#Text= tasted.
#Text=Paragidde, like to our Pears, and many more such like Fruits.
#Text=[Fruits common with other parts of India.]
#Text=Here are also, of Indian
#Text= Fruits, Coker-nuts; Plantins also and Banana  '  s of divers and sundry
#Text= sorts, which are distinguished by the tast as well as by the names;
#Text= rare sweet Oranges and sower ones, Limes but no Lemons, such as ours
#Text= are; Pautaurings, in tast all one with a Lemon, but much bigger
#Text= than a mans two fists, right Citrons, and a small sort of sweet
#Text= Oranges.
#Text=Here are several other sorts of Lemons, and Oranges, Mangoes
#Text=of several sorts, and some very good and sweet to eat.
#Text=In this sort
#Text= of Fruit the King much delights, and hath them brought to him from
#Text= all Parts of the Island.
#Text=Pine-Apples also grow there, Sugar Canes,
#Text= Water-Melons, Pomegranates, Grapes both black and white, Mirablins,
#Text= Codjeu  '  s, and several other.
#Text=There are three other Trees that must not here be omitted; Which
#Text= tho they bear no eatable Fruit, yet the Leaves of the one, and the
#Text= Juice of the other, and the Bark of the third are very renowned,
#Text= and of great benefit.
#Text=[The Tallipot; the rare Uses of the Leaf.]
#Text=The first is the Tallipot;
#Text= It is as big and tall as a Ships Mast, and very streight, bearing
#Text= only Leaves: which are of great use and benefit to this People;
#Text= one single Leaf being so broad and large, that it will cover some
#Text= fifteen or twenty men, and keep them dry when it rains.
#Text=The leaf being
#Text= dryed is very strong, and limber and most wonderfully made for mens
#Text= Convenience to carry along with them; for tho this leaf be thus broad
#Text= when it is open, yet it will fold close like a Ladies Fan, and then
#Text= it is no bigger than a mans arm.
#Text=It is wonderful light, they cut them
#Text=that they regarding not the seed, forthwith cut them down.
#Text=This Tree
#Text= is within a [The pith good to eat.]
#Text=Pith only, which is very good to
#Text= eat if they cut the Tree down before it runs to seed.
#Text=They beat it in
#Text= Mortars to Flower, and bake Cakes of it; which tast much like to white
#Text= bread.
#Text=It serves them instead of Corn before their Harvest be ripe.
#Text=[The Kettule yields a delicious juice.]
#Text=The next Tree is
#Text= the Kettule.
#Text=It groweth streight, but not so tall or big as a
#Text= Coker-Nut-Tree; the inside nothing but a white Pith, as the former.
#Text=It
#Text= yieldeth a sort of Liquor, which they call Tellegie: it is rarely
#Text= sweet and pleasing to the Pallate, and as wholsom to the Body,
#Text= but no stronger than water.
#Text=They take it down from the Tree twice,
#Text= and from some good Trees thrice, in a day.
#Text=An ordinary Tree will
#Text= yield some three, some four Gallons in a day, some more and some
#Text= less.
#Text=The which Liquor they boyl and make a kind of brown Sugar,
#Text= called Jaggory; but if they will use their skill, they can make it
#Text= as white as the second best Sugar: and for any use it is but little
#Text= inferior to ordinary Sugar.
#Text=The manner how they take this Liquor
#Text= from the Tree is thus; When the Tree is come to maturity, first out
#Text= of the very top there cometh out a bud, which if they let it grow,
#Text=little in general of them.
#Text=They serve both for Food, and for Carrees,
#Text= that is, sauce, or for a relish to their Rice.
#Text=But they make many
#Text= a meal of them alone to lengthen out their Rice, or for want of it:
#Text= and of these there is no want to those that will take pains but to
#Text= set them, and cheap enough to those that will, buy.
#Text=[The manner of their growing.]
#Text=There are two sorts of these Alloes;
#Text= some require Trees or Sticks to run up on; others require neither.
#Text=Of
#Text= the former sort, some will run up to the tops of very large Trees, and
#Text= spread out very full of branches, and bear great bunches of blossoms,
#Text= but no use made of them; The Leaves dy every year, but the Roots grow
#Text= still, which some of them will do to a prodigious bigness within a
#Text= Year or two  '  s time, becoming as big as a mans wast.
#Text=The fashion of
#Text= them somewhat roundish, rugged and uneven, and in divers odd shapes,
#Text= like a log of cleft wood: they have a very good, savoury mellow tast.
#Text=Of those that do not run up on Trees, there are likewise sundry sorts;
#Text= they bear a long stalk and a broad leaf; the fashion of these Roots
#Text= are somewhat roundish, some grow out like a mans fingers, which they
#Text= call Angul-alloes, as much as to say Finger-Roots; some are of a
#Text=white colour, some of a red.
#Text=Those that grow in the Woods run deeper into the Earth, they run up
#Text= Trees also.
#Text=Some bear blossoms somewhat like Hopps, and they may be
#Text= as big as a mans Arm.
#Text=[Boyling Herbs.]
#Text=For Herbs to boyl and eat with Butter they have
#Text= excellent good ones, and several sorts: some of them are six months
#Text= growing to maturity, the stalk as high as a man can reach, and being
#Text= boyled almost as good as Asparagus.
#Text=There are of this sort, some having
#Text= leaves and stalks as red as blood, some green: some the leaves green,
#Text= and the stalk very white.
#Text=[Fruits for sawce.]
#Text=They have several other sorts of Fruits which
#Text= they dress and eat with their Rice, and tast very savoury, called
#Text= Carowela, Wattacul, Morongo, Cacorebouns, &c. the which I cannot
#Text= compare to any things that grow here in England.
#Text=[European Herbs and Plants among them.]
#Text=They have of our English Herbs
#Text= and Plants, Colworts, Carrots, Radishes, Fennel, Balsam, Spearmint,
#Text=at the other; and before they can turn, will fill both bellies and
#Text= hands full, to carry away with them; and to stand all round to guard
#Text= their Fields is more than they can do.
#Text=This sort of Monkeys have
#Text= no beards, white faces, and long hair on the top of their heads,
#Text= which parteth and hangeth down like a mans.
#Text=These are so impudent
#Text= that they will come into their Gardens, and eat such Fruit as grows
#Text= there.
#Text=They call these Rillowes.
#Text=The flesh of all these sorts of Apes
#Text= they account good to eat.
#Text=There are several sorts of Squirrels also,
#Text= which they do eat when they can catch them.
#Text=Before I make an end of my discourse of their Beasts, it may be
#Text= worthwhile to relate the ways they use to catch them.
#Text=At which they
#Text= are very crafty.
#Text=[How they catch wild Beasts.]
#Text=For the catching of Deer or other wild
#Text= Beasts, they have this ingenious device.
#Text=In dark Moons when there
#Text= are drisling Rains, they go about this design.
#Text=They have a basket
#Text= made with canes somewhat like unto a funnel, in which they put a
#Text= potsheard with fire in it, together with a certain wood, which they
#Text= have growing there, full of sap like pitch, and that will burn like a
#Text=Alligators may be reduced hither: there be many of them.
#Text=Of which we
#Text= have said somewhat before.
#Text=[Kobbera-guion, a creature like an Alligator.]
#Text=There is a Creature
#Text= here called Kobbera guion, resembling an Alligator.
#Text=The biggest may
#Text= be five or six foot long, speckled black and white.
#Text=He lives most
#Text= upon the Land but will take the water and dive under it: hath a long
#Text= blew forked tongue like a sting, which he puts forth and hisseth and
#Text= gapeth, but doth not bite nor sting, tho the appearance of him would
#Text= scare those that knew not what he was.
#Text=He is not afraid of people,
#Text= but will ly gaping and hissing at them in the way, and will scarce
#Text= stir out of it.
#Text=He will come and eat Carrion with the Dogs and Jackals,
#Text= and will not be feared away by them, but if they come near to bark or
#Text= snap at him, with his tayl, which is about an Ell long like a whip,
#Text= he will so slash them, that they will run away and howl.
#Text=This Creature
#Text= is not eatable.
#Text=[Tolla-guion.]
#Text=But there is the Tolla guion very like the former,
#Text= which is eaten, and reckoned excellent meat.
#Text=The Chingulays say it
#Text= is the best sort of flesh; and for this reason, That if you eat other
#Text=flesh at the same time you eat of this, and have occasion to vomit, you
#Text= will never vomit out this tho you vomit all the other.
#Text=This creature
#Text= eats not carrion, but only leaves and herbs; is less of size than
#Text= the Kobbera guion, and blackish, lives in hollow Trees and holes in
#Text= the Humbosses: And I suppose is the same with that which in the West
#Text= Indies they call the Guiana.
#Text=[The People eat Rats.]
#Text=This Countrey has its Vermin also.
#Text=They have
#Text= a sort of Rats, they call Musk-Rats, because they smell strong of
#Text= Musk.
#Text=These the Inhabitants do not eat of, but of all other sort of
#Text= Rats they do.
#Text=Before I conclude my discourse of the Growth and Product of this
#Text= Countrey, it will not be improper to reduce under this head its
#Text= Precious Stones, Minerals, and other Commodities.
#Text=Of which I shall
#Text= briefly speak, and so make an end of this First Part.
#Text=[Precious Stones.]
#Text=In this Island are several sorts of Precious Stones,
#Text= which the King for his part has enough of, and so careth not to have
#Text= more discovery made.
#Text=For in certain places where they are known to
#Text=in other things.
#Text=The greatest part of the Inhabitants of the Land
#Text= are of the degree of Hondrews.
#Text=All Christians either White or Black are accounted equal with the
#Text= Hondrews.
#Text=The Whites are generally Honourable, only it is an abatement
#Text= of their Honour that they eat Beef, and wash not after they have been
#Text= at Stool; which things are reckoned with this People an Abomination.
#Text=[An Honour like unto Knighthood.]
#Text=Among the Noblemen may be mentioned
#Text= an Honour, that the King confers, like unto Knighthood; it ceaseth
#Text= in the Person  '  s death, and is not Hereditary.
#Text=The King confers it
#Text= by putting about their Heads a piece of Silk or Ribbond embroidered
#Text= with Gold and Silver, and bestowing a Title upon them.
#Text=They are
#Text= stiled Mundianna.
#Text=There are not above two or three of them now in
#Text= the Realm living.
#Text=[Goldsmiths, Blacksmiths, Carpenters, &c.]
#Text=Next after the degree
#Text= of Hondrews may be placed Goldsmiths, Blacksmiths, Carpenters and
#Text= Painters.
#Text=Who are all of one degree and quality.
#Text=But the Hondrews will
#Text= not eat with them: however in Apparel there is no difference; and they
#Text=are also privileged to sit on Stools, which none of the Inferior ranks
#Text= of People hereafter mentioned, may do.
#Text=Heretofore they were accounted
#Text= almost equal to the Inferior sort of Hondrewes, and they would eat
#Text= in these Artificers Houses, but afterwards they were degraded upon
#Text= this occasion.
#Text=It chanced some Hondrews came to a Smith  '  s Shop to
#Text= have their Tools mended, when it came to be Dinner time, the Smith
#Text= leaves work, and goes in to his House to dine, leaving the Hondrewes
#Text= in his Shop: who had waited there a great while to have their work
#Text= done.
#Text=Now whether the Smith fearing lest their hunger might move them
#Text= to be so impudent or desperate as to partake with him of his Dinner,
#Text= clapt to his Door after him: Which was taken so hainously by those
#Text= hungry People in his Shop, that immediately they all went and declared
#Text= abroad what an affront the Smith had put upon them.
#Text=Whereupon it was
#Text= decreed and confirmed, that for ever after all the People of that rank
#Text= should be deposed, and deprived of the Honour of having the Hondrewes
#Text= to eat in their Houses.
#Text=Which Decree hath stood in force ever since.
#Text=[The Privilege and state of the Smiths.]
#Text=Nevertheless these Smiths
#Text= take much upon them, especially those who are the King  '  s Smiths; that
#Text= is, such who live in the King  '  s Towns, and do his work.
#Text=These have
#Text=it.
#Text=That which makes these Smiths thus stately is, because the Towns
#Text= People are compelled to go to their own Smith, and none else.
#Text=And if
#Text= they should, that Smith is liable to pay Dammages that should do work
#Text= for any in another Smith  '  s Jurisdiction.
#Text=[Craftsmen.]
#Text=All that are of any Craft or Profession are accounted
#Text= of an inferior degree, as Elephant Catchers, and Keepers, who are
#Text= reckoned equal with the Smiths, &c. abovesaid, tho they neither eat
#Text= nor marry together; and these may wear Apparel as do the Hondrews,
#Text= and sit on Stools, but the Hondrews eat not with them.
#Text=No Artificers ever change their Trade from Generation to Generation;
#Text= but the Son is the same as was his Father, and the Daughter marries
#Text= only to those of the same Craft: and her Portion is such Tools as
#Text= are of use, and do belong unto the Trade: tho the Father may give
#Text= over and above what he pleaseth.
#Text=[Barbars.]
#Text=Next are are Barbars; both the Women and Men may wear
#Text= Doublets, but not sit on Stools, neither will any eat with them.
#Text=of the water goes into the Cloths and scalds them.
#Text=Then they take
#Text= them and carry them to a River side, and instead of rubbing them with
#Text= their hands, slap them against the Rock, and they become very clean;
#Text= nor doth this tear the Cloths at all, as they order it.
#Text=[Jaggory-Makers.]
#Text=Another rank after these are the Hungrams, or
#Text= Jaggory-Makers.
#Text=Tho none will eat with them, yet it is lawful to
#Text= buy and eat the Jaggory they make, (which is a kind of Sugar) but
#Text= nothing else.
#Text=[The Poddah.]
#Text=Another sort among them is the Poddah.
#Text=These are of no
#Text= Trade or Craft, but are Husbandmen and Soldiers, yet are inferior to
#Text= all that have been named hitherto.
#Text=For what reason neither I, nor,
#Text= I think, themselves can tell: only thus it falls to them by Succession
#Text= from their Predecessors, and so will ever remain.
#Text=[Weavers.]
#Text=After these are the Weavers.
#Text=Who beside their Trade,
#Text= which is Weaving Cloth, are Astrologers, and tell the People good
#Text= Days and good Seasons: and at the Birth of a Child write for them an
#Text= account of the day, time and Planet, it was born in and under.
#Text=These
#Text=accounts they keep with great Care all their Life-time: by which they
#Text= know their Age, and what success or evil shall befall them.
#Text=These People also beat Drums, and play on Pipes, and dance in the
#Text= Temples of their Gods, and at their Sacrifices; they eat and carry
#Text= away all such Victuals as are offered to their Idols.
#Text=Both which to
#Text= do and take, is accounted to belong to People of a very low degree
#Text= and quality.
#Text=These also will eat dead Cows.
#Text=[Basket-Makers.]
#Text=Next to the Weavers are the Kiddeas or
#Text= Basket-Makers.
#Text=Who make Fans to fan Corn, and Baskets of Canes,
#Text= and Lace, Bedsteds and Stools.
#Text=[Mat-Makers.]
#Text=Then follow the Kirinerahs.
#Text=Whose Trade is to make fine
#Text= Matts.
#Text=These Men may not wear any thing on their Heads.
#Text=The Women of
#Text= none of these sorts ever do.
#Text=Of these two last there are but few.
#Text=[The lower ranks may not assume the Habit or Names of the higher.]
#Text=All
#Text= below the Couratto or Elephant-Men, may not sit on Stools, nor
#Text= wear Doublets, except the Barbar, nor wear the Cloth low down their
#Text=and comes over their left shoulder, girt about with a belt of fine
#Text= pack-thread.
#Text=Their heads are shaved, and they go bare-headed and
#Text= carry in their hands a round fan with a wooden handle, which is to
#Text= keep the sun off their hands.
#Text=[Their Priviledges.]
#Text=They have great benefit and honour.
#Text=They
#Text= enjoy their own lands without paying scot or lot or any Taxes to the
#Text= King.
#Text=They are honoured in such a measure, that the people, where ever
#Text= they go, bow down to them as they do to their Gods, but themselves
#Text= bow to none.
#Text=They have the honour of carrying the Tallipot with the
#Text= broad end over their heads foremost; which none but the King does:
#Text= Wheresoever they come, they have a mat and a white cloth laid over
#Text= upon a stool for them to sit upon; which is also an honour used only
#Text= to the King.
#Text=[What they are prohibited.]
#Text=They are debarred from laying their hands
#Text= to any manner of work; and may not marry nor touch women, nor eat but
#Text= one meal a day, unless it be fruit and rice and water, that they may
#Text= eat morning and evening: nor must they drink wine.
#Text=They will eat any
#Text= lawful flesh that is dressed for them, but they will have no hand in
#Text=but only build a new house in their yard, like a Barn very slight,
#Text= covered only with leaves, and adorn it with Branches and Flowers.
#Text=Into
#Text= this House they bring some of the Weapons or Instruments, which are
#Text= in the Pagods or Temples, and place them on Stools at one end of
#Text= the house, which is hanged with Cloth for that purpose, and before
#Text= them on other Stools they lay Victuals: and all that time of the
#Text= Sacrifice there is Drumming, Piping, Singing, and Dancing.
#Text=[Who eat
#Text= the Sacrifices.]
#Text=Which being ended, they take the Victuals away, and
#Text= give it to those which Drum and Pipe, with other Beggars and Vagabonds;
#Text= for only such do eat of their Sacrifices; not that they do account such
#Text= things hallowed, and so dare not presume to eat them, but contrariwise
#Text= they are now looked upon as polluted meat.
#Text=And if they should attempt
#Text= to eat thereof, it would be a reproach to them and their Generations.
#Text=[Their Gods are local.]
#Text=These Spirits or Gods are local.
#Text=For those
#Text= which they worship in one County or part of the Land, are not known or
#Text= owned to have power over the People in other parts.
#Text=But each Countrey
#Text= hath several Spirits or Devils, that are peculiar to those places,
#Text= and do domineer over them, and are known by several names they call
#Text= them by: under whose subjection the People do acknowledge themselves
#Text=back.
#Text=There are also some baskets to put corn in, some mats to spread
#Text= upon the ground to sleep on: which is the bedding both for themselves
#Text= and friends when they come to their houses.
#Text=Also some Ebeny pestels
#Text= about four foot long to beat rice out of the husk, and a wooden Morter
#Text= to beat it in afterwards to make it white, a Hirimony or Grater to
#Text= grate their Coker-nuts with, a flat stone upon which they grind their
#Text= Pepper and Turmeric, &c.
#Text=With another stone which they hold in their
#Text= hands at the same time.
#Text=They have also in their houses Axes, Bills,
#Text= Houghs, Atches Chissels, and other Tools for their use.
#Text=Tables they
#Text= have none, but sit and eat on the ground.
#Text=[How they eat.]
#Text=And now we are mentioning eating, let us take a
#Text= view of this people at their meals.
#Text=Their Dyet and ordinary fare is
#Text= but very mean, as to our account.
#Text=If they have but Rice and Salt in
#Text= their house, they reckon they want for nothing.
#Text=For with a few green
#Text= Leaves and the juice of a Lemmon with Pepper and Salt, they will
#Text= make a hearty meal.
#Text=Beef here may not be eaten; it is abominable:
#Text= Flesh and Fish is somewhat scarce.
#Text=And that little of it they have,
#Text= they had rather sell to get mony to keep, then eat it themselves:
#Text= neither is there any but outlandish men, that will buy any of them.
#Text=It
#Text=is they indeed do eat the fat and best of the Land.
#Text=Nor is it counted
#Text= any shame or disgrace, to be a niggard and sparing in dyet; but rather
#Text= a credit even to the greatest of them, that they can fare hard and
#Text= suffer hunger, which they say, Soldiers ought to be able to endure.
#Text=[How the great men eat.]
#Text=The great ones have always five or fix sorts
#Text= of food at one meal, and of them not above one or two at most of
#Text= Flesh or Fish, end of them more pottage than meat, after the Portugal
#Text= fashion.
#Text=The rest is only what groweth out of the ground.
#Text=The main
#Text= substance with which they fill their bellies is Rice, the other things
#Text= are but to give it a relish.
#Text=[Discouraged from nourishing Cattel.]
#Text=If these people were not
#Text= discouraged from rearing and nourishing of Cattle and Poultry,
#Text= provisions might be far more plentiful.
#Text=For here are many Jackalls,
#Text= which catch their Hens and some Tigres, that destroy their Cattle:
#Text= but the greatest of all is the King; whose endeavour is to keep them
#Text= poor and in want.
#Text=For from them that have Hens his Officers take
#Text= them for the Kings use giving little or nothing for them; the like
#Text= they do by Hogs.
#Text=Goats none are suffered to keep, besides the King,
#Text=except strangers.
#Text=[Cleanly in dressing their meet.]
#Text=In dressing of their victuals they
#Text= are not to be discommended: for generally they are cleanly and very
#Text= handy about the fame.
#Text=And after one is used to that kind of fare,
#Text= as they dress it, it is very savoury and good.
#Text=They sit upon a mat
#Text= on the ground, and eat.
#Text=But he, whom they do honour and respect,
#Text= sits on a stool and his victuals on another before him.
#Text=[Their drink and manner of eating.]
#Text=Their common drink is only water:
#Text= and if they drink Rack, it is before they eat, that it may have the
#Text= more operation upon their bodies.
#Text=When they drink they touch not the
#Text= Pot with their mouths, but hold it at a distance, and pour it in.
#Text=They
#Text= eat their Rice out of China dishes, or Brass Basons, and they that
#Text= have not them, on leaves.
#Text=The Carrees, or other sorts of Food which
#Text= they eat with their Rice, is kept in the Pans it is dressed in,
#Text= and their wives serve them with it, when they call for it.
#Text=For it
#Text= is their duties to wait and serve their Husbands while they eat,
#Text= and when they have done, then to take and eat that which they have
#Text= left upon their Trenchers.
#Text=During their eating they neither use nor
#Text=earthen Pot, and set over the fire, and boil it so long, till it
#Text= becomes thick and black like Tar.
#Text=This they set by for their use,
#Text= and it will keep as long as they please.
#Text=A very small quantity of it
#Text= will suffice for sawce.
#Text=They call it Annego.
#Text=[Their sweet meats.]
#Text=They have several sorts of sweet-meats.
#Text=One
#Text= they call Caown.
#Text=It is like to a Fritter made of Rice-flower, and
#Text= Jaggory.
#Text=They make them up in little lumps, and lay them upon a Leaf,
#Text= and then press them with their thumbs, and put them into a Frying-Pan,
#Text= and fry them in Coker-nut Oyl or Butter.
#Text=When the Dutch came first to
#Text= Columba, the King ordered these Caown to be made and sent to them as
#Text= a royal Treat.
#Text=And they say, the Dutch did so admire them, that they
#Text= asked if they grew not upon Trees, supposing it past the Art of man
#Text= to make such dainties.
#Text=Oggulas another sort of sweet-meats, made of parched Rice, Jaggory,
#Text= Pepper, Cardamum, and a little Cinnamons.
#Text=They rowl them up in Balls,
#Text= which will grow hard.
#Text=These they tie up in bags and carry them with
#Text= them when they travail to eat in afternoons when they are hungry.
#Text=Alloways made much after the former manner, only they are flat in the
#Text= fashion of a Lozenge; which are good for faintings and thirsty souls
#Text= to relish their water, and to eat of in afternoons when they are at
#Text= home.
#Text=We carried some of these along with us in our travayl.
#Text=[A kind of Puddings.]
#Text=Tacpetties, made of Rice-flower, and the meat of
#Text= the Coker-nut and Jaggory.
#Text=They are made up into small lumps, and so
#Text= put in a Leaf, and laid on a cloth over a Pot of boyling water.
#Text=The
#Text= stream of which heats that which is laid upon it: and so they are
#Text= sodden like a Pudding.
#Text=They tast like white bread, Almonds and Sugar.
#Text=Pitu.
#Text=Which is made thus.
#Text=They take flower of Coracan, and sprinkle
#Text= a little water into it, being both put into a large Pot for the
#Text= purpose.
#Text=Then they stir and rowl it in the Pot with their hands: by
#Text= which means it crumbles into corns like Gun-Powder.
#Text=Then they have a
#Text= Pot of boyling water with a cloth tyed over it; and upon this cloth
#Text= they lay so much of this corn flower as they can conveniently cover
#Text= with another Pot.
#Text=And so the steam coming through the cloth boils it,
#Text= that it will be much like unto a Pudding.
#Text=And this they use to eat
#Text= as they do Rice.
#Text=[The Manner of their eating Betel-leaves.]
#Text=But to describe the
#Text= particular manner of their eating these Leaves.
#Text=They carry about with
#Text= them a small Box filled with wet Lime; and as often as they are minded
#Text= to eat Betel, they take some of this Lime, as much as they judge
#Text= convenient, and spread it thin upon their leaf; then they take some
#Text= slices of the Betel-nut, and wrap them up in the leaf, and so eat it,
#Text= rubbing their Teeth therewith ever and anon to make them black.
#Text=Thus
#Text= they eat it generally: but sometimes they eat it otherwise, according
#Text= as they please; neither spreading the Lime on the leaf, nor rolling
#Text= up slices of the Nut into it: But they will take a little of the Lime
#Text= out of their Box between their Fingers, and put it in their mouths,
#Text= and eat of the Nut and the Leaf by themselves.
#Text=But whensoever they
#Text= eat of the Betel-leaf, the Lime and the Nut always accompany it.
#Text=[How they make Lime.]
#Text=They have a pretty shift of making their
#Text= Lime, when they chance to need it as they are travailing.
